name: Endowment effect
aliases: Willingness to accept-willingness to pay disparity
statement: People demand more to give up something they own than they would pay to acquire it, so goods handed out at random tend to stay where chance put them.
meaning: Two experimental paradigms carry the name, and they do not measure the same thing. In the valuation paradigm one group is given a mug and states the lowest price at which it would sell, while another group states the highest price it would pay. The gap between the two is reported as a ratio of willingness to accept to willingness to pay. In the exchange paradigm everyone is handed one of two items of similar value and offered a swap. If ownership carries no weight, about half should trade. Loss aversion is the usual explanation for both patterns, and it is an explanation rather than the observation. The endowment effect is a measured asymmetry between owners and non-owners; loss aversion is a claim about the shape of a value function. This site keeps them in separate entries because the evidence for each is separate, and the coefficient argument belongs to the other one.

origin.where: Journal of Economic Behavior and Organization
origin.note: "Toward a positive theory of consumer choice" names it in one line: "Henceforth, I will refer to the underweighting of opportunity costs as the endowment effect." Thaler's evidence was two anecdotes, about a case of wine and a lawn, then a pair of survey questions about a fatal disease carrying a 0.001 risk, to which he says a typical answer was $200 to buy a cure and $10,000 to accept the same risk. He added two earlier studies, Weiss, Hall and Dong on schooling decisions and Becker, Ronen and Sorter on MBA students, and called the second inconclusive. He wrote that aside from Kahneman and Tversky's survey data there was "little in the way of formal tests". The laboratory demonstrations came a decade later.

evidence: Kahneman, Knetsch and Thaler ran the experiments the name now travels with. They first traded induced-value tokens, where each participant was told what the token was worth to the experimenter. Those markets cleared at the predicted volume, a ratio of actual to predicted trades of 1.0. The same people then traded consumption goods under the same rules, and across their first four experiments that ratio averaged .31. Experiment 5 switched to a randomly drawn price, which removes any incentive to shade a bid. Fifty-nine business statistics students at Simon Fraser took part, 29 potential buyers and 30 potential sellers. Fourteen and a half exchanges were expected and six occurred. The median selling price was $5.75 against a median buying price of $2.25, with means of $5.78 and $2.21. Experiment 6 added a third role. Seventy-seven Simon Fraser students were made sellers, buyers, or choosers, who picked between a mug and cash at each price. Twelve and a half trades were expected and three occurred, with median valuations of $7.12 for sellers, $3.12 for choosers and $2.87 for buyers. Experiment 7, with 117 students at the University of British Columbia, expected 19 trades and got one, at $7.00, $3.50 and $2.00. Sellers and choosers face objectively identical options, which rules out an income effect and locates the gap on the selling side. The exchange design comes from Knetsch in 1989, and his article was obtained and read for this entry. Three groups of University of Victoria students took part. Of 76 given a coffee mug and then offered a 400-gram Swiss chocolate bar, 89 percent kept the mug. Of 87 given the chocolate bar and offered a mug, 90 percent kept the bar. A third group of 55, holding nothing, split 56 percent for the mug against 44 percent for the bar. Horowitz and McConnell pooled the WTA and WTP literature. Their summary table headed weighted puts the mean ratio of accept to pay at 7.17 across 201 experiments, standard error 0.93, with observations weighted by the square root of the number of subjects. The often-quoted median of 2.60 sits in a different table, headed unweighted, and that table counts 206 ratios rather than 201. Tunçel and Hammitt published a second meta-analysis in 2014. Its abstract confirms the ordering by type of good and adds that the disparity is smaller under incentive-compatible elicitation and smaller in more recent studies. That full text was not obtained, so no pooled ratio from it is quoted here.

replication.headline: Plott and Zeiler made the mug gap vanish in 2005 by tightening how values were elicited, two other laboratories reproduced that null, and a third running the same procedures found a ratio of 2.53.
replication.detail: Plott and Zeiler argued that the gap is an artefact of subject misconceptions about the mechanism used to elicit values. They first ran the Kahneman, Knetsch and Thaler procedure and reproduced the gap: mean willingness to pay $1.74 against mean willingness to accept $4.72, with 29 subjects on each side and a Wilcoxon z of -4.8. They then added anonymity, an incentive-compatible mechanism, training and paid practice rounds. Pooled across three sessions, mean willingness to pay was $6.62 from 36 buyers and mean willingness to accept was $5.56 from 38 sellers, so the buying figure was the higher of the two. No session rejected equality, with Wilcoxon p values of 0.9368, 0.3536 and 0.0821, and 0.2050 pooled. Their 2007 paper did the same for the exchange paradigm across five treatments, every one tested one-tailed. Baseline procedures, with 64 mug owners and 65 pen owners, gave 84 percent of mug owners and 28 percent of pen owners choosing mugs, p = 0.00. With the full set of controls, 69 mug owners and 70 pen owners, the two figures were 54 and 67 percent, p = 0.94 for an asymmetry in the predicted direction and 0.06 for one in the reverse direction. Two of the five treatments produced an asymmetry at the 5 percent level. Isoni, Loomes and Sugden replied in 2011 that lottery data from the same 2005 study, left out of that paper, showed a disparity that persisted, and that their own new data confirmed both the missing mug gap and the lottery gap. Plott and Zeiler answered in the same issue that all the mug data reject endowment effect theory and that lottery gaps come from shifting beliefs about the lotteries. Brown and Cohen ran both sets of procedures with and without anonymity, and report that the conventional ones produce gaps and the Plott and Zeiler ones do not. Fehr, Hakimov and Kübler then ran the Plott and Zeiler protocol at the Technical University of Berlin with 191 students, 95 in the mug sessions and 96 with a USB stick. Mean willingness to pay for the mug was 1.34 euros against a mean willingness to accept of 3.39 euros, a ratio of 2.53. The USB stick gave 3.54 against 5.60. Both t tests are one-tailed, t = 5.01 and t = 4.08, each p < 0.01. They then used dominated bids in the practice lotteries to find the people who plainly understood the mechanism. The 42 of 95 who never bid outside the bounds on any of the 16 lotteries, 23 buyers and 19 sellers, still gave 1.48 against 3.02, a ratio of 2.04, p < 0.015. Their conclusion is that misconceptions are not the main source of the gap. Klass and Zeiler argued in the UCLA Law Review that legal scholarship went on relying on endowment theory after experimental economists had stopped. In the field, Fehr and Kübler embedded the exchange design in the German Socio-Economic Panel. Of 3,223 households approached, 3,146 took part, and 2,807 of those were handed either a towel or a notebook and offered a swap at the end of the interview. The overall trading rate was 32 percent, 38 percent among those given the towel and 28 percent among those given the notebook, against a benchmark near 50. The other 339 chose between the two items without being endowed, and split 42 percent towel to 58 percent notebook. Trading was unrelated to their measure of loss aversion, and telling people in advance that a swap would be offered moved the rate from 32.7 to 32.4 percent. The largest test located is by Chapman, Dean, Ortoleva, Snowberg and Camerer, four incentivised surveys of representative United States samples totalling 4,000 adults, using lottery tickets rather than goods. Mean willingness to accept over willingness to pay was 2.07 and the median 1.18.

study.cite: Fehr, D., Hakimov, R., & Kübler, D. (2015). The willingness to pay-willingness to accept gap: A failed replication of Plott and Zeiler. European Economic Review, 78, 120-128.

limits: The effect belongs to inexperienced traders more than to people in general. List took the exchange design to the floor of a sportscard show, endowing people with a Cal Ripken ticket stub or a Nolan Ryan certificate, and ran it on 148 subjects, 74 dealers and 74 non-dealers. Dealers traded at 43.6 and 45.7 percent in the two endowment directions, close to the 50 percent benchmark, while non-dealers traded at 20.0 and 25.6 percent. Splitting the non-dealers at six trades a month, just above their mean of 5.66, sharpens it: 14 of 30 experienced non-dealers traded, 46.7 percent, against 3 of 44 inexperienced ones, 6.8 percent. His panel models find that trading experience raises the probability of trading even once individual heterogeneity is controlled, and that the heterogeneity is itself significant, so both experience and selection are at work. No preregistered replication of the mug experiment was located, and no multi-laboratory preregistered replication of either paradigm. Crossref, which carries AEA RCT Registry records, and the open web were searched on 17 August 2026 and returned none. The closest thing is the Fehr and Kübler field experiment, registered as AEARCTR-0003992 with a pre-analysis plan. No journal version of that paper appeared in Crossref at this check, so it is cited as a discussion paper, and the Chapman study was also still a working paper. The Horowitz and McConnell figures come from the August 1999 University of Maryland working paper. The 2002 journal article sits behind Elsevier's paywall, three attempts at open copies failed, and only its abstract was read.
misreadings: The commonest error is to treat a mug result as a measurement of loss aversion. Gächter, Johnson and Herrmann ran two endowment experiments on 660 customers of a German car manufacturer, 300 of them between subjects and 360 within. Only the 360 also took the lottery task, so only they yield both measures from the same person. Their published paper puts the Spearman correlation between riskless and risky loss aversion at 0.677, with riskless the higher of the two on average. Correlated is not identical, and a valuation gap constrains the coefficient only loosely. The second error is quoting 7.17 as the size of the endowment effect. It is Horowitz and McConnell's weighted mean across every kind of good, and it is pulled up by public and non-market goods at 10.41 across 46 experiments and health and safety at 10.06 across 32. Ordinary private goods, the category mugs and pens sit in, give a weighted mean of 2.92 across 59 experiments. The unweighted median is 2.60. The third is reading Thaler's coinage as a claim about attachment to possessions. He defined it as the underweighting of opportunity costs, which is a claim about how a forgone gain is booked rather than about affection for an object. The fourth is treating Plott and Zeiler as having settled the question, and the fifth is treating them as isolated. Their argument is about experimental procedure, and it was contested inside the American Economic Review by Isoni, Loomes and Sugden. Those same authors reproduced the missing mug gap under the Plott and Zeiler procedures, as did Brown and Cohen, and Fehr, Hakimov and Kübler are the published attempt that did not.
